expectations.description: Does NOT validate the supervisor's conclusion that lower alpha in the inpatient sample means the scale performs less reliably or should be restricted to mild-to-moderate populations
expectations.evidence: The response explicitly states 'The drop in α shows the scale is less reliable in severe populations' is 'Overstated' and explains that 'The drop likely reflects ceiling effects and range restriction, not true reliability failure.' It further clarifies that calling it a 'reliability failure conflates two distinct constructs' and that the supervisor's mechanistic explanation is 'incomplete and can mislead.'

expectations.description: Identifies the ceiling effect as the cause: the inpatient mean of 26.4/30 indicates nearly everyone scores near the maximum, compressing variance and suppressing alpha regardless of item quality
expectations.evidence: The response explicitly identifies the ceiling effect: 'Your inpatient sample has a mean of 26.4 out of 30 on a 10-item scale... Individual items have almost no room left to vary. When nearly everyone endorses most items at their maximum, item variances collapse. Collapsed item variances → attenuated inter-item correlations → lower α. This is a floor/ceiling artifact, not evidence of measurement failure in any fundamental sense.'

expectations.description: Explains the mechanism: alpha depends on inter-item correlations, which are attenuated when everyone endorses items at the same high level — this is a variance problem, not an item-quality problem
expectations.evidence: The response explicitly states: 'Collapsed item variances → attenuated inter-item correlations → lower α. This is a floor/ceiling artifact' and 'Range restriction reliably depresses observed correlations — this is a statistical artifact' and formula shows α depends on ratio of item variances to total variance. The mechanism (variance restriction → attenuated correlations → lower alpha) is clearly explained as a variance/artifact problem distinct from item quality.

expectations.description: States that the causal direction of the supervisor's inference is backwards: lower alpha in severe samples is an expected artifact of ceiling effects, not evidence that the scale works worse in that population
expectations.evidence: The response explicitly states: 'The drop likely reflects ceiling effects and range restriction, not true reliability failure' and frames the supervisor's reasoning as backwards — lower alpha in severe samples is an artifact of ceiling effects and range restriction ('floor/ceiling artifact'), not evidence the scale works worse. The table explicitly labels the supervisor's claim as 'Overstated' and explains the causal direction: collapsed item variances → attenuated inter-item correlations → lower α, driven by statistical artifacts of truncated range.

expectations.description: Notes that reliability is a property of scores in a specific sample — a scale can have valid items that perform well in severe populations but still show low alpha due to ceiling-effect range restriction
expectations.evidence: The response explicitly states: 'Cronbach's α is not a fixed property of a scale. It is a function of both the items and the score variance in the specific sample' and explains that range restriction 'reliably depresses observed correlations — this is a statistical artifact, not a signal that the items are measuring something incoherent.' It also notes 'If you drew a random subsample from your community sample and artificially truncated it to only those scoring 24–30, you would almost certainly see a similar drop in α, with the same scale and same items, simply because of reduced variance' — directly addressing that reliability is sample-dependent and that valid items can show low alpha due to ceiling-effect range restriction.

expectations.description: Recommends IRT as the appropriate method for evaluating scale performance at the severe end of the trait: item information functions show where on the theta range items are most discriminating, regardless of floor/ceiling issues in a specific sample
expectations.evidence: The response explicitly recommends IRT analysis: 'IRT analysis (e.g., Graded Response Model) — plot the test information function across the latent trait continuum. You'll likely find the scale has high information in the mild-to-moderate range and drops off sharply in the severe range, which is the real story.' It also mentions item information functions conceptually when discussing that 'α reflects average reliability across the full score range, but what you really want to know is whether the scale provides good measurement precision (test information) in the severe range.'
